title: The Stop That Does Not Need the App: A Latched Onboard Stop Path Driven by the Robot's Own Clock

questions.question: The application crashes while the robot drives. Which stop works?
options: A stop on the robot, driven by the robot's own loop and clock, that treats the missing heartbeat as the signal
The stop button in the application, since it has priority over other messages
The operating system, which stops any robot whose application has crashed
A stop message sent by the station's second process
questions.explanation: A stop that depends on the application cannot work when the application is what failed. The robot's own loop notices that the heartbeat has gone.

questions.question: A guard compares the age of the last message when each message arrives. Messages stop. What does it do?
options: Stops after the timeout, as designed
Stops at once, since the last message is now old
Raises an error and waits for the operator
Nothing: with no messages nothing ever looks, and the last command stays (0.8 at 5 s in the test)
questions.explanation: The check only runs when a message arrives. With none arriving it never runs, so the last command stays in force.

questions.question: The e-stop loop has never been reported on, and heartbeats arrive. Is the robot allowed to move?
options: Yes: heartbeats show the station is alive
No: an unreported loop is an open loop, and the robot starts stopped
Yes, at reduced speed, until the loop is reported
Only if the application says the loop is closed
questions.explanation: The robot starts stopped, and a loop it has not heard from is treated as open. Each thing that lets it move has to be shown, not assumed.

questions.question: The link comes back after the stop. What should the robot do?
options: Stay stopped until a deliberate reset, which needs a closed loop and a fresh heartbeat
Move at once: the reason for the stop has gone
Move slowly until the operator confirms
Ask the application whether to continue
questions.explanation: A robot that starts moving by itself when a link returns surprises whoever walked up to it. Leaving a stop is a decision, and it is refused unless the loop is closed and a heartbeat is fresh.

questions.question: Why is a clock that goes backwards treated as a stale heartbeat?
options: A backward clock is always a sign of a hardware fault
Because the timeout is stored as an unsigned number
To keep the log's time stamps in order
now minus the last beat goes negative and would pass a greater-than-timeout test for as long as the clock stays behind
questions.explanation: With the clock set back, the age of the last beat is negative and never exceeds the timeout. Treating that as stale keeps the robot from trusting a heartbeat for ever.

questions.question: Why is this software not the whole answer for a machine that can hurt someone?
options: It only works at 100 Hz
It depends on a network being present
If the control loop that calls it hangs, nothing calls it: the same idea has to exist in hardware that does not run your code
It cannot tell a pressed button from a cut wire
questions.explanation: This code runs inside the robot's control loop. If that loop stops, so does the stop path, which is why a hardware watchdog and a brake that applies itself are also needed.
